Say the word "spoon" to yourself fifteen times. By the tenth or eleventh repetition, something strange happens: the word detaches from the thing. Spoon. Spoon? Spoon. It becomes pure sound—noise that English speakers have agreed to exchange for a small utensil with a bowl at one end. The object stays solid in the drawer; the word goes soft and surreal in your mouth.

Linguists call this semantic satiation, and I find it quietly wonderful, because it reveals something about language we normally can't see. Words feel like natural extensions of the things they name, as if "tree" grew on trees. But they're not. They're conventions, agreements, small acts of collective imagination that we all maintain without noticing. Every conversation is a feat of coordination: I make noises with my mouth, you find meaning in them, and somehow we stay in sync.

There's a loneliness hiding in this, admittedly—we can never verify that my "blue" matches your "blue," or that my sadness feels like yours. But there's something better there, too: meaning works at all. These arbitrary sounds, pushed through air, carry grief and grocery lists, love poems and instructions for building bridges. Language is a scheme so absurd that if it didn't already exist, no one would dare invent it.

So every so often, take a common word and say it until it falls apart. Not to break it—just to admire the pieces, and to remember that this whole miracle runs underneath every sentence, all the time.
